title: ICMR Survey Puts Anaemia at 56% of Women, Severe Cases Below 2%
excerpt: SAMPADA, ICMR's venous-blood survey of more than 2 lakh people across 183 districts, finds most anaemia is mild and iron deficiency explains only about half of cases among women and children.
body:
• ICMR's SAMPADA survey (2023-2025), covering more than 2 lakh people in 183 districts, found anaemia in 56% of women of reproductive age, 46% of adolescent girls and 42% of children aged 12-59 months — lower than previous national surveys, the Council said.
  • Most cases are mild: severe anaemia was found in less than 2% of people across most age groups, and about half of anaemic women, adolescent girls and children have mild anaemia.
  • Iron deficiency accounts for roughly half of anaemia cases among women, adolescent girls and children; vitamin B12 and folate deficiency levels were similar in anaemic and non-anaemic people, pointing to other causes including infections and haemoglobinopathies.
  • SAMPADA measured haemoglobin from venous blood on automated analysers — the method matters, because the last national figures (NFHS-5, 2019-21: 57% of women, 67.1% of children aged 6-59 months) came from a survey whose blood-collection method the government had questioned.

India's newest national nutrition survey puts anaemia prevalence below earlier national estimates, with severe cases rare. The Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) has released key findings from SAMPADA — the Survey for Assessment of Markers of Population Health, Activity, Diet and Anthropometry, conducted in 2023-2025 — showing anaemia in 56% of women of reproductive age, 46% of adolescent girls aged 10-19, and 42% of children aged 12-59 months, according to the official release carried by ANI. Among adolescent boys and men aged 20-59, prevalence was 22-23%.

SAMPADA covered more than 2 lakh individuals from over 81,000 households across 183 districts in 35 states and union territories, and analysed more than 1.7 lakh blood samples for haemoglobin. It is among the world's largest nutrition surveys, ICMR said, and for the first time gives nationally representative estimates for older adults.

Why the method matters

A key feature of SAMPADA is venous blood sampling with automated analysers, which ICMR said provides greater accuracy and reproducibility. The distinction is central to how the new numbers should be read. The previous national benchmark, the National Family Health Survey-5 (2019-21), reported 57% of women aged 15-49 and 67.1% of children aged 6-59 months as anaemic — figures the government later set aside amid concerns about the reliability of its blood-collection method, as Mirror Now reported in its coverage of the debate over anaemia policy. Public health experts had been pressing for SAMPADA's release precisely because India lacked updated, venous-blood-based figures.

Mostly mild, and not only about iron

The majority of cases are mild. About half of anaemic women — including pregnant and lactating women — adolescent girls and children have mild anaemia, and among adolescent boys, adult men and older men roughly three-fourths of those affected are mild cases. Severe anaemia was observed in less than 2% of people across most age groups. Iron deficiency accounts for approximately half of anaemia cases among women, adolescent girls and children, and is concentrated in those life stages. Vitamin B12 and folate deficiency prevalence was similar among anaemic and non-anaemic individuals, indicating a limited contribution from those deficiencies, while infections, haemoglobinopathies and inflammation linked to chronic disease also need to be addressed, the survey found.

"It is encouraging that prevalence of anaemia is lower in SAMPADA compared to previous national surveys. The comprehensive anaemia profiling in SAMPADA survey provides an evidence base to strengthen the ongoing national efforts towards Anaemia Mukt Bharat."

— Dr Rajiv Bahl, Secretary, Department of Health Research and Director General, ICMR

What happens next

ICMR said the findings support targeted, population-specific approaches rather than uniform interventions: people with moderate and severe anaemia have a higher prevalence of iron deficiency and need to be identified through testing, treated and tracked until resolution, as envisaged under Anaemia Mukt Bharat 2.0. Dr Bharati Kulkarni, Director of ICMR-NIN, said the evidence can guide prevention and management across life stages while identifying where further research and improved surveillance are required. For families, the practical reading is narrow but useful: anaemia remains common — more than half of women of reproductive age — but the severe end of the condition, the part that most urgently needs treatment, affects under 2% in most age groups.
nri_angle: The venous-blood survey resets the anaemia numbers diaspora families cite when elderly parents and children in India are tested, and targets treatment at moderate and severe cases.
